triggers.action: Clear the drains and inlets; the level should already be at or below the limit; open all wells.
The reservoir must be nearly empty; open all wells and stop topping up from roof tanks.
The reservoir must be empty when it starts; open all wells, stop topping up from roof tanks, clear every inlet.
Beyond the 135 mm design: the reservoir cannot hold this even if empty; expect water to leave the lease.
Stress storm: well beyond the reservoir; protect buildings and the road; the plan cannot hold it.

notes: Every number comes from the 125-year IMD daily record and the planner assumptions; nothing is calibrated on site. The daily grid understates short intense rain.

The risk calendar and the free-space rule use the observed record directly (largest day of each month, 1-in-10-year month). Return periods of the forecast classes and the design storm come from the GEV fit of the annual maximum days (100-year day about 135 mm); Gumbel was rejected for this record.
Potable-quality water from the reservoir needs treatment; the model does not include treatment or its losses.
Treated wastewater is assumed to be 80 % of domestic use with 90 % recovery (72 % of the daily use); it is used first for flushing, irrigation and the fountain.
Water above the reservoir volume is counted as leaving the lease. The two first years of the record are dropped as a start-up period.
Water drawn down to the recharge wells to keep the free space is not counted as supply: the earlier M7d runs show little retention in an open aquifer.
Monthly reference evaporation, crop factor, planted area, fountain size and persons per flat are assumptions to be replaced with measured or design values.
Well yield and sustainable abstraction are not tested: the outside-supply figure is a requirement, not a promise that the wells can deliver it.

Roof wetting: the one-storm sizing (net zero plan, one storm, season of storms) applies the roof coefficient to all the rain, with no wetting loss - the safe side for sizing the reservoir. The day-by-day views (risk calendar and drought, closed loop) take the first 1 mm of each rain day off the roof and the road before the coefficient - the safe side for supply. Over the 125-year record this gives about 13 % less roof water a year than no wetting loss.
